newsitem.title: MALI: Mali might accept U.S. veto of Boutros-Ghali.
newsitem.headline: Mali might accept U.S. veto of Boutros-Ghali.

text.p: Mali signalled on Tuesday it could accept a U.S. veto of Boutros Boutros-Ghali's reappointment as U.N. secretary-general provided the job went to another African.
Foreign Minister Dioncounda Traore stated Mali's position after talks between U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Malian President Alpha Oumar Konare.
"Officially, what I could say now is that he (Boutros-Ghali) remains Africa's candidate," he told a news conference with Christopher.
But he added: "I must stress the essential point for us is that Africa have a second mandate as the head of the U.N. This is really the most important issue for all African countries."
Mali previously unequivocally endorsed the 73-year-old Egyptian secretary-general, dismissed by Washington as unfit to lead the world body into the 21st century.

Mali's redefined position appears more in line with that of the Organisation of African Unity, which officially backs Boutros-Ghali while holding the door open for another candidate should Washington make good its veto threat. Some countries like Niger have already made known their candidates.
The issue of the U.N. job is high on the agenda of Christopher's five-nation Africa tour, the first by a U.S. secretary of state to the region for more than six years.

Another topic is how to pressure Nigeria's ruling generals to speed the country's transition to democracy. Christopher said as he headed for Mali on Monday that he would seek a consensus for further sanctions against the Nigerian government, on top of limited ones imposed by the West.

Nigeria angered the international community by hanging nine opposition activists last November in defiance of appeals for clemency. The military government was already under censure for aborting democratic elections in June 1993.
Christopher pointedly left out the regional giant from his circuit, starting his tour in impoverished Mali as a tribute to its own smooth change from one-party dictatorship to democracy.
At the news conference, Traore stressed Mali's support for human rights and opposition to imposing an oil embargo on Nigeria.
U.S. officials said Christopher discussed Nigeria with Konare and Traore but they did not agree on a way forward.

Christopher said Konare agreed to join a U.S. initiative for an all-African force to respond to humanitarian crises in Africa. Other officials said the president did not commit specific troops because the initiative is still being drafted.
Traore made an impassioned plea for Africa's right to a second tenure of the top U.N job.

"Please trust Africans. We have the means to contribute to the U.N. How can you the international community trust us with your confidence? By giving us a second term as head of the U.N. This is really what is essential to us," he said.
Christopher said on Monday: "Everywhere I go, I'm going to be talking about the importance of Africa coming forward with good candidates for the U.N. secretary-generalship."

U.S. officials said they believed Malian leaders heard the U.S. message that the U.N. post could be lost to Africa if they did not drop their support for Boutros-Ghali, whose term expires on December 31.

Christopher announced that U.S. Peace Corps volunteers would soon return to northern Mali because of Konare's success in ending ethnic conflict in that region. He announced a $1 million U.S. aid package to help demobilize and retrain Tuareg rebels in the region and $700,000 to help Mali prepare for its second democratic election in 1997.
Christopher leaves Mali on Wednesday for Ethiopia. He later visits Tanzania, South Africa and Angola.
